The Croatian DPA announced two administrative fines. The main one, HRK 2.15 million, was imposed on a telecommunications provider that failed to take appropriate technical and organisational security measures, so that an attacker gained unauthorised access to the personal data of about 100,000 data subjects. The provider itself reported the breach under Article 33 and informed its users. The second, HRK 30,000, was imposed on a car sales and service centre in Zagreb for failing to mark premises under video surveillance (national law, not the GDPR). The text is a press release, not the full decision.

A former employee complained to the Italian DPA that her ex-employer, Stay Over s.r.l., answered her access request late and inadequately, and kept her work email account active after she left, forwarding incoming mail to other staff without proper information. The Garante found the processing unlawful under the GDPR and the Italian Code. It banned further processing of data extracted from the account (apart from storage for legal defence), ordered the company to bring its IT-tools policy into line with data protection rules within 60 days, and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

During an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software, the Garante checked Clio S.r.l., which supplies a SaaS whistleblowing platform to public and private clients. Some clients had never appointed Clio as processor under Art. 28 GDPR, and Clio kept no record of processing activities carried out as processor. The Garante found processing without a valid legal basis (Arts. 5, 6 GDPR, Art. 2-ter Code) and a breach of Art. 30(2). It fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective measures as the conduct had ended.

During an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software, the Garante inspected the supplier Clio S.r.l. and found that the municipality of Ginosa used its platform without having appointed the supplier as processor under Article 28 GDPR. The municipality only regularised this in November 2019, and a real report had been handled through the platform since March 2018. The Garante found that making the whistleblowing data available to the supplier without a valid legal basis was unlawful processing. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000, ordered publication of the decision, and adopted no corrective measures because the conduct had ceased.

The Garante ran an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software and inspected the provider Clio S.r.l., finding that the water utility Acqua Novara.VCO used the application without appointing the provider as data processor. The company used the platform from 3 July 2019 and only formalised the Article 28 appointment on 3 December 2019. The Garante found unlawful processing (no valid legal basis for making whistleblowing data available to the provider, and no Article 28 arrangement). It fined the company EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The charge about not communicating the DPO's contact details was dropped, and no corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

The Italian DPA held that a website operator used Google Analytics without implementing adequate safeguards for U.S. data transfers as required by Article 46 GDPR. The operator was reprimanded and ordered to bring the data transfers into compliance or cease them altogether.
The Greek DPA imposed a €150,000 fine on Vodafone PANAFON S.A. for the lack of appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect the security of its electronic communication services.

The Finnish DPA reprimanded a bank for violating Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 17(1)(a) GDPR by not responding to the data subject's request to have their data deleted when it was no longer necessary for processing.

The Belgian DPA held that discussing a data subject's health-related personal data in a staff meeting where she was absent and consequently including the data in the minutes of the meeting was incompatible with the purpose of the original processing (personnel management) and did not have any other legal basis to rely on.
The Spanish DPA fined a telecommunications provider €3,000 for sending out marketing correspondence despite the data subject's repeated objections.

A debtor complained that a claims management company kept phoning her about debts for which a court had already discharged her under the over-indebted households law. She had objected and asked for erasure, but the company refused to deal with the requests on the grounds that it could not identify her. The Authority found that the processing had no legal basis and breached the lawfulness and accountability principles, and that the company unjustifiably obstructed the exercise of her rights. It imposed two fines of EUR 10,000 each, EUR 20,000 in total.

The Danish DPA reprimanded the largest Danish retail group for violating Article 32(1) GDPR by storing passwords in plain text which made personal data accessible to unauthorised persons. It also ordered the controller to inform the affected data subjects about the data breach.

A non-profit organisation, Homo Digitalis, complained on behalf of a data subject that Clearview AI, a US company selling a facial recognition tool built on images scraped from the internet, had not answered her access request. The company claimed the GDPR did not apply to it, said it had no EU establishment, and did not attend the hearing. The Authority found breaches of the principles of lawfulness and transparency (Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 9) and of Articles 12, 14, 15 and 27. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000,000 and ordered the company to comply with the access request. It also banned collection and processing of data of persons in Greece using its facial recognition methods and ordered deletion of such data.

The Hungarian DPA imposed a €1,228 fine on a hotel booking service for sending direct marketing emails without a valid legal basis and not complying with data subject rights under Articles 12, 15, 17 and 21(2) GDPR.
the DPA finds that the contested decision, including but not limited to the complaints of the data subject, correctly established the facts of the case and qualified the administrative offence.

The Danish DPA reprimanded a processor for violating Article 32(1) GDPR by storing user passwords in plain text and allowing access to its system via single-factor authentication only. The processor was ordered to make appropriate changes.

The Romanian authority completed an investigation in May 2022 into E Software Concept SRL. Invoices and airway bills containing customers' personal data, including usernames and passwords, were publicly accessible via links on the company's website. The company was fined EUR 3,000 equivalent for inadequate security measures and EUR 1,000 equivalent for not supplying the information the authority requested. Total fines are therefore about EUR 4,000 (in lei).

A US medical-device company notified a personal data breach: an email about the Eversense XL glucose monitoring system for people with diabetes was sent to about 2,000 Italian recipients with all addresses visible in the 'cc' field instead of 'bcc'. The Garante's investigation also looked at the company's Eversense app and found problems with legal bases, transparency, privacy notice content and a late appointment of an EU representative. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, fined the company EUR 45,000, ordered corrective measures on the privacy notice and legal bases within 90 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A life insurer, while paying out a different policy, mistakenly entered the wrong policy number because an operator mistyped the last digit. It sent automated payment notices containing the complainant's name, policy number and amount paid to two unrelated beneficiaries. The insurer only learned of this months later, after the complainant reported it, and did not treat it as a breach to notify. The Garante found a breach of the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and of integrity and confidentiality, and fined the company EUR 20,000. It also ordered publication of the decision.
The Italian DPA issued a warning against TikTok for processing cookies without the users' consent under its announced privacy policy update.
The Spanish DPA fined an amateur football association €3,000 because its website lacked a privacy policy despite the fact that it collected various personal data.

The Polish DPA held that the Polish Chief National Surveyor violated Articles 33(1) and 34(1) GDPR by not notifying the DPA and the data subjects after it had accidentally disclosed land and mortgage register numbers on its website.

The Polish DPA held that a medical facility violated Articles 33(1) and 34(1) GDPR by not notifying the DPA and the data subject of a data breach after accidentally disclosing the data subject's personal data to another patient.

The Croatian DPA held that a controller installed a video surveillance system monitoring the public space without a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR and ordered the controller to adjust the angle of the cameras.

A member of the sommelier federation FISAR complained that the national council's decision to exclude him was shared with all members through the minutes of its meeting. The Garante found that the internal rules allow publication of disciplinary measures only once they are final. This measure was not final and was later annulled by the arbitration board, yet it was still circulated and stayed on the members' cloud platform until 28 January 2022. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f) and 6(1) GDPR and fined the non-profit association EUR 5,000. No further corrective measures were ordered because FISAR had published a correction.
Medical research: green light from the Italian Garante for 'step-by-step' consent
The Croatian DPA reprimanded the Center for Social Welfare for violating Articles 5 and 6 GDPR by publishing its employees' personal data on its bulletin board.
The DPA imposed a fine of €3,000 on a child psychologist for not satisfying an access request in a complete and timely manner in violation of the provisions of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA held that a there is a conflict of interest when a DPO is simultaneously also a company's senior lawyer, deputy CEO or board member. However, a DPO can hold the position of compliance officer.

After the data subject had withdrawn a complaint, the Hellenic DPA continued with an ex officio investigation into the sending of unauthorized advertising messages and issued a reprimand on the controller for violation of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.

The Danish DPA held that an access request was excessive because it concerned over a million documents not related to the data subject as an individual. Therefore, the controller did not have to act on the request according to Article 12(5)(b) GDPR.

The Danish DPA reprimanded an insurance company for violating Articles 25(1) and 32(1) GDPR by lacking sufficient security measures and not implementing privacy by design in the development stages of their customer portal.

The Spanish DPA fined Naturgy Energy Group €80,000 for disclosing a customer's personal data to a third party and changing her registered email address without her consent. The DPA held that Naturgy failed to adopt the necessary security measures and violated the principle of integrity and confidentiality.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Swedish DPA reprimanded Nordax Bank for violations of Articles 12(3), 12(6), 15 and 17 GDPR. The bank had not complied with several requests of the data subject. The DPA also ordered the bank to comply with these requests.
The Spanish DPA fined a public broadcaster (Radiotelevision Española) €30,000 for failing to disguise the voice of a rape victim before publishing an audio recording of her testimony at trial.
The Finnish DPA issued a warning to a healthcare provider whose envisaged risk profiling of patients for scanning and prevention purposes violated Articles 6, 9 and 22 GDPR.
The Danish DPA reprimanded a fashion brand because its lack of sufficient technical and organisational measures allowed hackers to gain access to the customers' payment information.

The Danish DPA reprimanded the Danish Health Data Authority for violating Article 32(1) GDPR by not testing its medication database for service architecture errors, which led to a data breach affecting 267 data subjects.

The Danish DPA reprimanded a consumer electronics retailer for violating Article 32(1) GDPR by not deleting personal data on a used TV or storing the TV sufficiently securely before such deletion, which enabled access to the data by an unauthorised third party.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation on 27 May 2022 into a homeowners' association following a complaint about security guards collecting data from people entering a residential complex. The association had its guards record identity details of delivery staff and couriers in an access register without a justified legal basis and without proof of proper information. It also kept CCTV images for about a year and a half without setting a retention period. Two fines were imposed (RON 9,885.80 and RON 24,714.50, i.e. EUR 2,000 and EUR 5,000, total EUR 7,000), plus corrective measures under Art. 58(2)(d).
The Icelandic DPA rejected a complaint for lack of evidence which alleged that the Icelandic postal service unlawfully processed personal data by maintaining a special register for stamp collectors.

The Belgian DPA held that it could not establish a breach of professional secrecy pursuant to Article 55(3) GDPR as only a judge was competent to do so. It could not, therefore, find the data obtained from the complainant's criminal record to be unlawfully obtained.

The Belgian DPA held that a publisher (De Tijd) lawfully refused a data subject's request for erasure regarding a news article on the data subject in the publisher's online archive, based on it's right to freedom of expression and information.

The Italian DPA fined UniCredit S.p.A. €70,000 for requiring that a data subject submit their access request via a designated form, and for not providing all information required under Article 15 GDPR.

A customer complained to the Garante that Deutsche Bank had not answered his access request and request for a copy of the privacy notice, sent by certified email in July 2020, and also complained about a credit-bureau report made without prior warning. The bank only replied after the Authority intervened, in June 2021. The Garante pursued only the unanswered rights request, rejected the bank's arguments (the request was buried in a longer letter; the customer already had the notice), and found a breach of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR. It fined the bank EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA ordered Google LLC to de-index an article about a criminal investigation on the data subject, as there was no public interest regarding the news, regardless of the article being accurate and up to date.
The Austrian DPA held that the sending of letters inviting data subjects to get a covid-19 vaccine did not consitute a violation of data subject's rights under Austrian Data Protection Law.

The Norwegian DPA has banned the use of "Shinigami Eyes" on Norwegian territory after determining violations of Article 6(1), Article 12(2) and Article 14 GDPR. The controversial browser addon allows users to highlight trans-friendly or transphobic social network pages and users.

In this Article 60 GDPR procedure, a data subject filed two rectification requests and an access request at Klarna Bank AB, a Swedish payment provider. Klarna had used incorrect first names in invoices for online purchases made by the data subject and their partner. The Swedish DPA only determined a violation of Article 15 GDPR because the controller answered to an access request 1 year and 3 months after it was originally submitted.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Danish DPA reprimanded Danske bank for a violation of Article 32(1) GDPR. A technical error resulted in the unauthorised disclosure of invoices to business customers of the bank.

The Austrian DPA rejected a complaint against a district court acting as land registry court, holding that including an unredacted divorce settlement in the public land register's document collection was legally mandated.

A debt collection company, acting as processor for Sky Italia, found an email address on the web that it wrongly believed belonged to a debtor. It sent two emails about his unpaid Sky debt to a different person, an employee of the debtor's company. The debtor complained to the Garante. The Garante found a breach of the lawfulness, fairness and data minimisation principles and of the legal basis requirement. It fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication. No corrective orders were imposed because the conduct had ended and measures had been put in place.

Italy's DPA reprimanded a website operator for failing to provide appropriate safeguards for the transfer of personal data to the US through Google Analytics, ordering it to comply with Article 46 GDPR or suspend data transfers to Google LLC.

The Italian DPA issued a reprimand to the municipality of Brindisi for failing to fully comply with the GDPR rules regarding the concealing of data pertaining to a man and his son's legal proceedings against the aforesaid municipality.

The Italian DPA held that Google LLC was not obliged to de-list search results linking to particular news articles, as the publication of the relevant information was in the public interest since it concerned ongoing judicial proceedings.
The Austrian DPA dismissed a complaint concerning the recording of a private phone call without consent. The activity was considered to fall under the household exception of Article 2(2)(c) GDPR.

The Finnish DPA found a life insurance company to have breached Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, Article 9 GDPR and Article 25(2) GDPR for not having a legal basis to process the health data of life insurance applicants and for processing the data unnecessarily.
The Finnish DPA found a life insurance company to have breached Article 9 GDPR for not having a legal basis to process the health data of life insurance applicants.

The Finnish DPA held that an insurance company violated the fairness, data minimisation and data protection by default principles, among others, by requesting the entire medical record of the data subject from their healthcare provider to determine the insurance company's liability.

The Finnish DPA held that a BMW dealership did not have to disclose the service history of a used vehicle to a new buyer under Article 15 GDPR because it contained the personal data of the previous owner, not the new one.

The complainant's mobile number was assigned for four days in September 2019 to a third party who had the SIM migrated and a new SIM issued in a shop, while the complainant's SIM was deactivated. This is a new merits procedure after an earlier decision (fine of EUR 25,000) was withdrawn during an appeal. The Litigation Chamber found that the telecom operator had not verified identity adequately, so did not take sufficient security measures, and did not notify the breach to the authority. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000 for breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2), 24, 32, 33(1) and 33(5) GDPR. A note at the top says the Market Court rejected the appeal against this decision on 22 February 2023.

The Slovenian DPA found that a controller-processor arrangement was not an accurate description of the responsibilities shared by a cloud computing provider and its clients because both made determinations about the purposes and means of processing; the DPA ordered the cloud computing provider to establish joint-controller arrangements with its clients.
The Croatian DPA determined that a school violated Articles 25 and 32 GDPR by losing the master diploma and exam certificate of a former student.

The Finnish DPA ordered a hospital to delete any historical data, location logs, and other employee personal data generated by Windows 10 for Workstations. One of the OS features violated the "data protection by default" principle under Article 25(2) GDPR.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation on 27 May 2022 into a homeowners' association running a residential complex. Security guards recorded couriers' and delivery staff's names, ID details and visit times in an access register without a justified legal basis or proper information, which was excessive. The association also kept CCTV images for about a year and a half without setting a retention period. The association was fined two amounts (EUR 2,000 and EUR 5,000 equivalent, in lei) and ordered to review its measures, set retention periods and apply data minimisation.

The Romanian DPA fined a building owners association €7000 for keeping an extensive register of couriers entering the residential complex and for keeping video surveillance footage of the entrance longer than necessary for security purposes.

The Italian DPA found that ASL Roma 1 had published on its transparency web page two provisional registers of access requests, covering over a thousand requests, showing requesters' names and details of the health documents requested. The ASL said it was a material error: the working file was uploaded instead of the anonymised final one. The Garante held that this breached the ban on disseminating health data, data minimisation and the lawfulness rules. It fined the ASL EUR 46,000, ordered publication of the decision, and imposed no further corrective measures because the conduct had ended.

A customer complained that a branch of Intesa Sanpaolo gave her bank account movement data to her parent, who was no longer authorised to access it since she had come of age. The bank said an employee acted in good faith because he knew the parent personally (a retired bank employee). The Garante rejected the good-faith defence, found the disclosure to an unauthorised third party unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(f) and 6 GDPR, and fined the bank EUR 100,000. The Garante also ordered publication of the decision.

A former executive of the municipality of Afragola complained that his CV, including his home address, mobile number and private email addresses, stayed on the municipality's transparency web page and in search engines after the legal publication period ended, and that his objection request went unanswered. The Garante found the data were published without legal basis and with excessive content, and that the municipality answered the request late and without giving the required information. The municipality's defence that its external provider was at fault was rejected, since the controller remains responsible. A fine of EUR 10,000 was imposed, with publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

A complaint was filed because the Università Agraria di Nettuno published on its website a resolution naming the complainant, a former extraordinary commissioner, in connection with legal action to recover pay. The Garante found that the online dissemination had no adequate legal basis and breached the lawfulness and minimisation principles, even though the entity relied on transparency duties. It fined the entity EUR 4,000, banned any further online dissemination of the complainant's data, required a report within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision. The complaint about not appointing a data protection officer was dropped.

The Italian DPA fined the website www.inelenco.com 50,000€. Among many GDPR infringements, this online telephone directory had no legal basis and processed and published the data of 357,046 data subjects without their knowledge and consent.
The Italian DPA ordered Facebook Italy and Meta Platforms Ireland Limited to remove revenge porn material relating to a data subject from its platforms.

Following a thematic investigation by the Inspection Service into cookies on popular Belgian news sites, the Litigation Chamber examined the Knack and Le Vif websites of Roularta Media Group. It found non-essential and statistical cookies placed without consent, pre-ticked boxes for partners' cookies, inadequate and partly wrong cookie information, storage-limitation problems, withdrawal of consent that did not work, and a disclaimer denying responsibility for third-party cookies. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 50,000 and ordered Roularta to bring the processing into compliance within three months and prove it.

The Norwegian DPA fined the Labour and Welfare Administration €486,700 for publishing CVs and confidential personal data of 1,8 million data subject online without a legal basis, in breach of Articles 6(1), (3) and Article 5(1)(a), and 5(1)(f) GDPR.

In an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Norwegian DPA ordered an HR-services provider, pursuant to Article 58(2)(d) GDPR, to provide the data subject with information he requested in an access request (Article 15 GPDR).
In an Article 60 procedure, the Danish DPA determined that Trustpilot did not have to comply with an access request since Trustpilot was a mere processor under Article 28 GDPR.

Pursuant to the Article 60 GDPR cooperation mechanism, the Berlin DPA held that a photographer breached Article 6(1) GDPR for lacking a valid legal basis for the publication of data subject's photos on their website. The GDPR derogation for journalism under German law, which is granted under Article 85(2) GDPR, did not apply as the publication mainly served a commercial purpose.

Following a complaint, the Romanian authority investigated a debt-collection company that had disclosed a data subject's personal data, including health data from medical leave certificates, to doctors and medical units with which she had no legal relationship. It found breaches of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and a late notification of the security incident under Article 33. The controller was fined 24,740 lei (about EUR 5,000) for the first group of breaches and received a warning for Article 33. The text is a press release, not the full decision.

The Croatian High Administrative Court held that the surveillance system of a multi-property building was set up in accordance with the GDPR and national law, which required two-thirds of the co-owners to authorise the use of the system.
The Greek DPA has ruled on its incompetence to examine communication confidentiality violations that were falling outside the scope of the GDPR
The Slovenian DPA held that a private entity offering SARS CoV-2 tests violated Article 13 GDPR by failing to inform data subjects about transferring their data to a third party.

The Austrian DPA authorized the transfer of personal audit documents to the US Public Company Accounting Oversight Board following an application for approval by the Federal Minister of Finance. The transfer was based on an administive arrangement per Article 46(3)(b) GDPR.

A sole trader (a retired consultant) complained that the Labour Inspection Authority had run a credit check on his one-person business while investigating another company he had worked for. Datatilsynet found that the Working Environment Act § 18-5 did not give a sufficient supplementary legal basis under Art. 6(3) for obtaining credit information about a person not under inspection, from a third party. It held the infringement intentional, since the inspector deliberately ran the check, and imposed a fine of NOK 150,000. The order to establish internal routines was dropped because Arbeidstilsynet submitted new routines banning credit checks in supervisory cases. A reprimand was issued in a separate decision.

The Hungarian DPA held that the Budapest Bar Association violated Article 15 and Article 12 GDPR by failing to timely reply to an access request. The fact that the Association's offices were closed had no relevance on the deadline.

Pursuant to the Article 60 cooperation mechanism, the Swedish DPA held that a controller violated Article 12(3) GDPR by not responding to an Article 15 GDPR access request within the one month time limit. However, taking into account all the circumstances of the case, the DPA considered this as a minor infringement and did not impose a fine.

The Danish DPA also issued a reprimand against the Syddansk Universitet for violating security requirements under Article 32 GDPR by accidentally making 400 personal files accessible to more than 7,000 employees for a period of two weeks. The university also had no access log to check who accessed the information during that time period.

The Guardia di Finanza inspected a shop in Rosta (Turin) in March 2019 and found a video surveillance system with 12 cameras, 4 of them working, with no information signs and no authorisation from the Labour Inspectorate or union agreement. The Garante opened sanction proceedings; the owner submitted no defence and did not cooperate. The Garante declared the processing unlawful for breach of Articles 5 and 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A former employee of the municipality of Villabate complained that the municipality sent a letter about the garnishment of part of his salary to his new employer, disclosing alleged debts and the reasons he left. He also complained that the municipality had not properly appointed a data protection officer (DPO) or published the DPO's contact details. The Garante found that the disclosures to the bank and the new employer had no valid legal basis, and that the municipality appointed its DPO late, chose a person in a conflict of interests, and failed to communicate and publish the DPO's contact details. It fined the municipality EUR 6,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ceased.

The Danish DPA issued a reprimand against the Danish Trade Union and Unemployment Fund for breaching Articles 5(1)(d) and 32 GDPR by accidentally disclosing a data subject's new name to her violent former partner.

In a procedure under Article 60 GDPR, the Swedish DPA reprimanded Klarna Bank AB for not providing information on the recipients to which personal data had been disclosed when replying to an access request under Article 15 GDPR.

The Finnish DPA fined a magazine publisher €85,000 for deficiencies in facilitating the exercise of data subject rights. The controller, among other things, required data subjects to print, fill, sign and send a paper form to have their data deleted.

The DPA ordered the Police University College to give the data subject a video recording featuring other students. The DPA held that the controller wrongfully denied the right of access under Article 15(4) GDPR without sufficiently demonstrating how giving the copy would adversely affect others.
The Belgian Data Protection Authority ordered a company to comply with Article 13(1)(b) GDPR and to publish the contact details of their DPO on their website.

Following a complaint, the Romanian authority investigated a financial institution that had installed audio-video cameras in employees' offices. It found the controller had not shown that the stated purpose was justified, that less intrusive means had failed first, or that it met the principles of Article 5 and the lawfulness conditions of Article 6 GDPR and Article 5 of Law 190/2018. The controller was fined RON 19,772.4 (about EUR 4,000).

In October 2020 the Belgian railway company SNCB emailed holders of the free Hello Belgium Railpass a message mixing Covid-19 health advice with promotion of travel destinations, with no easy way to opt out. The Inspection Service found no valid legal basis and no facilitated right to object. The Litigation Chamber rejected the SNCB's reliance on contract performance and its argument that the email was not direct marketing. It found breaches of Articles 5, 6, 12 and 21 GDPR and fined SNCB EUR 10,000, noting the very wide reach (3.6 million Railpasses). The Market Court later reduced the fine.

The Finnish DPA also held, among the others, that it lacked competence under Article 55(3) GDPR to supervise the Supreme Court's criminal case disclosure policies because the court acted in its judicial capacity.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation in March 2022 into Megareduceri TV S.R.L. after several complainants received unsolicited commercial SMS messages on their personal phone numbers promoting a website, without having consented. The company confirmed receipt of the authority's requests but did not answer them, so it was fined for failing to provide the requested information. The fine was 19,795.6 lei (about EUR 4,000). The authority also ordered corrective measures to ensure processing complies with the GDPR and that phone numbers are not used for direct marketing without prior express consent.

This is the follow-up decision on the fine in the Seesaw student system case. An earlier decision of 16 December 2021 had found that the City of Reykjavík's processing of schoolchildren's personal data in Seesaw breached data protection law, and had ordered the accounts closed and the data deleted. In this decision Persónuvernd decided whether to impose an administrative fine and how much. It considered the City's objections point by point under the Article 83(2) factors. It imposed a fine of ISK 5,000,000, payable within a month. The decision stresses that children's data was involved, that sensitive data was likely to be entered, and that data was transferred to the US without adequate safeguards.

A doctor complained that HEI – Medical Travel had obtained, stored and used his email address for a marketing email, and had not handled his access request. HEI's employee had copied doctors' email addresses from the closed area of the Icelandic Medical Association's website using a relative's doctor login. Persónuvernd found there was no legal basis for the processing and that the access request breached Article 15 GDPR, since the data was deleted after the request and no access was given. It imposed an administrative fine of ISK 1,500,000.

The Belgian DPA held, among others, that a controller is not obliged to report a data breach which results from listing the recipients of an email in CC instead of BCC if the email is only received by a small group (16 people).
The Finnish DPA fined a telemarketing company €8,300 for not giving the data subject access to the sales call recording even after the DPA ordered it to do so.

An employee of a provincial fire service administration complained that her superior inspected the browsing history on her work computer without informing her, and that her access request for copies of disciplinary decisions was not answered. The Authority found the Fire Service Headquarters, as controller, in breach of the principles of lawfulness, transparency and security, of the rules on the data protection officer's involvement, and of the right of access. It ordered compliance measures and a reply to the access request, and imposed three fines totalling EUR 35,000.

The Italian DPA held that the controller had no legal ground to inform the parents of the children enrolled in a private nursery school about the pregnancy of a teacher. The DPA also held that this was a violation of the principles of lawfulness and data minimization.

An employee of the Ministry of Defence complained about two disclosures of his data. In the first, health-related information (a court ruling reference, a request for medical checks and a medical visit summons) was passed to the president and a member of a competitive-exam board. In the second, an email with criminal-proceedings data was mistakenly forwarded to a serviceman who had no right to it. The Garante found that both disclosures lacked a legal basis and breached Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 9 and 10 GDPR and Articles 2-ter, 2-sexies and 2-octies of the Code. It fined the Ministry EUR 10,000, ordered publication of the decision, and imposed no corrective measures given the Ministry's assurances and new procedures.

A publisher's digital legal-news service posted in full a Court of Cassation order on the same-sex adoption of a minor, with the identifying details of the family, despite the court's annotation requiring anonymisation. The family complained to the Garante, also about an incomplete answer to their access requests. The Garante found the processing unlawful, banned further processing, issued a warning for the incomplete and late reply to the data subject rights request, and imposed a fine of EUR 40,000. The publisher had removed the order the day after the request and cooperated.

Nos, a telemarketing agency working for Vodafone, bought about 3.8 million contact records from two UK list providers and passed them on to Vodafone as an autonomous controller. It gave the individuals no information notice and obtained no consent for the disclosure. The Garante rejected Nos's argument that it acted only as Vodafone's processor. It found violations of Articles 13, 14, 5(1)(a), 6 and 7 GDPR, banned further processing of the acquired data and fined Nos EUR 20,000. The fine was kept low because the company was inactive and going into liquidation.

The hospital notified two data breaches in which newsletters to patients of its neurology unit and its transplant and bariatric surgery unit were sent with recipients' email addresses in the visible CC field instead of BCC. This revealed to recipients that others were patients of those units, i.e. health information. The Garante rejected the hospital's arguments, found a breach of Art. 5(1)(f) and Art. 9 GDPR, and fined it EUR 70,000. No corrective orders were issued since the conduct had ended and remedial measures were taken. The decision is to be published in full.

The Italian DPA fined a municipality €3,000 for publishing the names of an excluded candidate of a competition procedure on its website without a legal basis and for rejecting the candidate's request for erasure.

The Italian DPA fined a public waste collection company (processor) €200,000 for installing video surveillance systems without prior authorisation of the Municipality of Taranto (controller) and for posting videos on Facebook with identifiable persons without a legal basis.

The Italian DPA fined a daily newspaper €40,000 for negligently publishing the personal details of a homosexual couple and their adopted child in an online article covering related judicial proceedings.

The Spanish DPA held that sending someone notifications regarding monetary fines directed at another person constitutes a violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. As the respective data was not rectified in time after receiving a complaint, it also resulted in a breach of Article 32 GDPR.

The Danish DPA confirmed that a children shelter's use of unsecure communication, such as SMS, to process a child's personal data was justified because the child's custodian was not available through any other means, and the child's interest in being admitted into the shelter outweighed data protection concerns.

The Spanish DPA fined the owner of a commercial website €1,800 for processing personal data and using of cookies without a legal basis and for not providing sufficient information to the data subject per Article 13 GDPR.

The Danish DPA reprimanded a municipality for violating Article 32(1) GDPR by not restricting terminated employee's access to its file system and not following up with control over the former employee's access rights.

The Norwegian DPA held that shareholders are entitled to information under Article 14 GDPR when their personal data is processed by shareholder managers, and issued a reprimand against a company, ordering it to provide a data subject with this information.
The claimant exercised his rights of access and deletion. The right of access was granted. However, the right for deletion could not be granted in accordance with Article 17 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA fined a website provider €5,000 for listing personal data of lawyers on its website without a legal basis and without informing the data subjects. In addition, its privacy and cookie policy were not compliant with the GDPR.

The Danish DPA reprimanded the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority (FSA) for breaching Article 32(1) GDPR by passing on information about whistleblowers to a journalist. The disclosure resulted from an inadequate anonymisation technique when email addresses could still be revealed from redacted PDF documents.

The Data Protection Authority decided that cases concerning camera surveillance by neighbours are to be dealt with by the police, due to the Act of March 2007 (regulating the installation of surveillance cameras).

The Spanish DPA issued a fine of €1800 against an online clothes store for processing personal data without data subjects' consent, for failing to have a privacy policy, and for the use of non-essential cookies without providing appropriate information through a cookie banner.

The French DPA issued a fine of €1,500,000 against a software solutions provider acting as a processor for medical analysis laboratories, due to a data breach concerning the data of almost 500,000 data subjects in violation of Articles 28, 29, and 32 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined an adult content website €8000 for its unlawful use of cookies and providing insufficient information related to their nature and purposes, as well for having an outdated privacy policy, which was based on data protection laws prior to the entry into force of the GDPR.

The Austrian DPA held that the operator of a search engine must delete a link to a database which contains the home address of the data subject if the latter fears for his physical integrity after receiving a death threat.

The Romanian DPA issued a €500 fine against a neighborhood owners association for failing to cooperate with the DPA by not providing requested information related to an investigation regarding video surveillance recordings, in violation of Article 83(5)(e) GDPR.

The Dutch DPA investigated the Fraude Signalering Voorziening (FSV), a fraud-signalling application used by the Tax and Customs Administration until February 2020. It found that the Minister of Finance, as controller, processed personal data in FSV from 4 November 2013 to 27 February 2020 without a legal basis, without a specified purpose, with inaccurate data and with excessive retention. It also found inadequate security (access, logging and log checks) and that the data protection officer was not involved properly or in time in the DPIA. The AP imposed six separate administrative fines totalling EUR 3,700,000, raising the base amounts for the nature, gravity and duration of the breaches, negligence, the data categories and, for some, earlier relevant infringements.

During an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software, the Garante checked a hospital in Perugia and its provider ISWEB. It found the hospital processed personal data via the whistleblowing application without a specific privacy notice, without recording it in the register of processing, without a DPIA, and without adequate security (navigation logs kept on firewalls, credentials of a departed RPCT still active). It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 13, 14, 25, 30, 32 and 35 GDPR and fined the hospital EUR 40,000. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ended and the hospital had cooperated.

During an inspection campaign on whistleblowing software, the Garante examined ISWEB S.p.A., which supplies a whistleblowing platform to clients including the Perugia hospital and acts as their processor. ISWEB used a hosting provider (Seeweb) without a proper Article 28 arrangement, both for its own processing as controller and for processing done for clients as processor, including without the hospital's prior authorisation. ISWEB argued the breaches were merely formal and that the IP addresses involved were not personal data, but the Garante rejected this. It found the Article 28 infringements, fined ISWEB EUR 40,000, ordered it to bring the processing into compliance within 30 days and report back, and ordered publication of the decision.

A commercial agent complained that the company cut off her work email account without notice, kept it alive, and ignored her requests for access to her data. The company also failed to answer the Garante's information requests, so the Garante used the Guardia di Finanza to serve them. The Garante found breaches of fairness and storage limitation, of the duty to inform, of the access right and response deadlines, and of the duty to answer the authority. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered access for the complainant, deactivation of the account with automatic notices, a ban on further processing of the extracted data and better procedures, and fined the company EUR 50,000.

A individual complained that Made in Italy s.r.l.s. called him twice for promotion without consent and ignored his access, erasure and objection requests. The company also never answered the Garante's request for information and did not defend itself. The Garante found breaches of Articles 15, 17, 21, 6 and 7 GDPR and of the Code (Art. 130(3), 157). It issued a warning, ordered the company to answer the complainant, banned further processing of his data, and fined it EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.

A debtor complained that the bank Findomestic contacted his wife, who was guarantor on only one of his loans, about another loan for which he alone was liable. The bank explained that a staff member mistakenly entered the wife's phone number as a contact, so two SMS messages about payment status were sent to her in October 2020. The Garante found the processing unlawful and in breach of the principles of lawfulness, fairness, transparency and data minimisation. It fined the bank EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A man who had bought goods from the company asked it on 10 July 2020 for access to his personal data and related information under Article 15 GDPR, and the company did not answer within the legal time limit. During the procedure the company only listed categories of data, called the request unfounded and pretextual, and argued the data were already known to him and belonged to his firm. The Garante rejected these arguments, since the request concerned his own personal data, and found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15. It ordered the company to reply to the data subject within 30 days and fined it EUR 10,000.

The Garante received a report that the café 'Caffè Antica Roma', run by Rebirth s.r.l., had a non-compliant video surveillance system. The company ignored two requests for information, so the Guardia di Finanza inspected and found 14 working cameras with no information signs and no labour inspectorate authorisation or union agreement. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Articles 114 and 157 of the Code, and fined the company EUR 15,000, also ordering publication of the decision.

After a report about a video surveillance system at the company's premises, the Guardia di finanza inspected in November 2021 and found 15 working cameras. Signage was missing in several areas, two cameras exceeded those authorised by the labour authority (authorisation was requested only in 2018 for a 2013 installation), and the three people with access to the footage shared credentials and only one had been instructed. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and (c), 13, 29 and 32 GDPR and Article 114 of the Code, rejected the argument that employee consent cured the problem, and fined the company EUR 10,000. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

The municipality of Orte was fined €20,000 by the Italian DPA for operating photo-traps without adopting any compliance measures, for failing to provide information to the data subjects, and for failing to provide direct contact to their DPO.

The Danish DPA proposed that Danske Bank should be fined €1,345,000 for lack of storage and erasure procedures in over 400 systems containing the personal data of millions of data subjects. The police will investigate the case before a final decision is made in the courts.

Following press reports, the Belgian DPA investigated the use of thermal cameras and a second-line health check at Brussels Airport to screen passengers for COVID-19 in 2020. The Litigation Chamber found that the airport company and its contractor (the first-aid company running the second-line check) lacked a valid legal basis for the processing of health data, and that the airport company breached transparency duties and the data protection impact assessment rules. It fined the airport company EUR 200,000 and the contractor EUR 20,000, and reprimanded the airport company for finalising its impact assessment late. The decision was later partly annulled (first defendant) and wholly annulled (second defendant) by the Market Court.

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber examined the use of thermal cameras by Charleroi airport to check passengers' temperature during COVID-19. It found there was no adequate legal basis for processing health data, and that transparency and information duties were breached. The DPIA was carried out three months after the processing began and was inadequate. It imposed a EUR 100,000 fine and a reprimand for shortcomings in the processing register. The decision was later partly annulled by the Market Court.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, thermal cameras at Brussels Airport (Zaventem) screened passengers for a temperature above 38°C. Ambuce Rescue Team then carried out a second check, a symptom questionnaire. The Litigation Chamber found that the airports had no valid legal basis for processing this health data, and it also found shortcomings in the information given to travellers and in the impact assessments. It fined Ambuce Rescue Team EUR 20,000, alongside fines of EUR 200,000 on Zaventem and EUR 100,000 on Charleroi. A note on the page says the Market Court later annulled the decision entirely as regards Ambuce Rescue Team.

A customer complained that Piraeus Bank kept sending account-movement alerts (Winbank Alerts) for her debit card to an e-mail address belonging to a third person with the same name, and did not fix it after being told. The bank said the joint account holder had registered an address differing only by a dot, which Gmail treats as identical, and that no breach occurred. The Authority found the bank breached confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(f)) and its duties to notify the breach to the Authority and the data subject (Arts. 33 and 34). It fined the bank EUR 10,000 in total and issued a warning to put in place technical and organisational measures to verify e-mail addresses given for alerts.

A head of department at a municipality complained that the former mayor, now a municipal councillor, sent letters containing her personal data to many recipients, including trade unions, after she chose to be appraised by the new mayor. The former mayor argued that he acted under public authority (Art. 6(1)(e)) and for legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)). The Authority found that sending the letters to the municipal employees' union and to the national federation of municipal employees (POE-OTA) breached the lawfulness principle of Art. 5(1)(a) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 on him as controller.

A former managing director and employee complained against his ex-employer, which had restored and analysed the mailboxes from his work laptop after dismissal and refused his requests for erasure, restriction and objection. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of lawfulness and minimisation (Art. 5(1)(a), 6(1)(f)), information duties, data subject rights (Arts 15, 17, 18, 21) and Art. 28. It ordered compliance with the complainant's requests, introduction of a policy charter and an end to processing data older than 5 years, and imposed a fine of EUR 7,500. The Market Court later partially annulled the decision.
